title: Types of Bonds

brief.h: Corporate bonds and the Trust Indenture Act
brief.md:
- **Corporate bonds** = debt of commercial/industrial issuers raising money for expansion. Term usually means **maturities of at least 10 years**; **notes** = medium-term; **commercial paper** = corporate paper of **no more than 270 days**.
- Trading is mostly **over-the-counter (OTC)**, not on exchanges.
- **Tax**: interest is **fully taxable as ordinary income** at federal, state **and** local level.
- **Trust Indenture Act of 1939**: corporate debt issues of **more than $50 million** need a written **trust indenture** between issuer and an **independent trustee** acting for bondholders.
- Indenture contains **protective covenants** (promises by the issuer): submit SEC filings, pay taxes, no selling of key assets, maintain insurance, maintain a certain credit profile.
- The **trustee** (typically a large bank) acts in the bondholders’ best interest and, on default, may **seize and sell the issuer’s assets** to repay holders.
> **Exam tip** Covenants protect **bondholders**, never the issuer. The $50 million threshold is *more than*, and the Act covers corporate debt, not municipal bonds.

brief.h: Secured vs unsecured debt and liquidation priority
brief.md:
- **Secured debt** = backed by corporate collateral; holders have rights to it on default.
  - **Mortgage bonds**: secured by real estate / real property.
  - **Collateral trust bonds**: secured by financial assets the company owns (stocks, bonds, other securities).
  - **Equipment trust obligations**: secured by equipment (airplanes, trucks, trains).
- **Unsecured debt = debentures** (synonyms). Backed only by the issuer’s “good faith”; **pays more interest** than secured debt (greater credit risk).
- Unsecured debt can be contractually **senior** to other unsecured debt; the junior piece is **subordinated debt**, lower priority in bankruptcy, so it **pays more interest**.

| Priority in bankruptcy (paid in full before next class) | Risk / expected return |
|---|---|
| 1. Secured bondholders | Least risky / lowest |
| 2. Unsecured bondholders and general creditors | |
| 3. Subordinated debt and convertible bonds | |
| 4. Preferred stockholders | |
| 5. Common stockholders | Riskiest / highest |

- Lower priority = greater risk = **higher expected return**.
> **Exam tip** All bondholders rank ahead of **all** equity holders. Debentures are *unsecured*, not “secured by the company’s name”.

- Investor may convert the bond into a **fixed number of common shares** of the issuer; terms are in the **indenture**.
- **Lower coupon** than a comparable non-convertible bond from the same issuer (investor pays for the conversion option).
- Issuer benefits: **lower fixed borrowing costs** and **no immediate dilution** of common shares (versus issuing equity).
- Investor view: **safer than common stock**, can deliver stock-like returns, **less volatile than stock**. Price floor = the price at which its yield equals that of a similar non-convertible bond.
- Because it can convert at any time it **trades more like equity**; with **stable interest rates** its price is **more volatile than other debt** because it moves with the **underlying stock**.
- **Conversion price** = stated price per share at which conversion occurs. **Conversion ratio** = shares received, **always based on par**, regardless of market price.
- **Parity price** = value at which the investor is **indifferent** between holding the bond and converting (no profit/loss at conversion).
- Liquidation: ranks with **subordinated debt**.
> **Exam tip** Conversion ratio = **$1,000 par ÷ conversion price**. The bond’s current market price is a distractor.

brief.h: Eurodollar bonds and corporate secondary market
brief.md:
- **Eurodollar bond**: issued **outside the US**, **denominated in US dollars**; issued and traded outside the US and **not registered with the SEC**. Used to make securities more marketable when the home currency is unstable.
- **Eurodollar deposit**: US dollars held in a **bank abroad** (e.g., a dollar account at a Swiss bank). Different instrument!
- The **secondary market** for fixed income is the **largest financial market in the world** and is **OTC** (banks, broker-dealers, trading by computer/phone) — unlike equities, mainly exchange-traded.
- Large companies may have **dozens or hundreds** of different bond issues, so each bond trades **less often** than the issuer’s stock; the **bid–ask spread is wider** to compensate dealers for holding risk.
- Liquidity differences between two corporate bonds depend more on **credit rating** than on coupon or maturity.
> **Exam tip** Bond = issued abroad in dollars. Deposit = dollars in a foreign bank. Keep them apart.

- Largest debt issuer in the world; backed by **full faith and credit** of the US (taxing power, ability to print currency). Safest securities; **pay less interest** than corporate and municipal debt.
- **Tax**: interest **taxable federally, exempt from state and local** income tax.
- Sold at **auction** (to large investors, then trade OTC); a **noncompetitive tender** guarantees an individual’s order is filled.
- **Five marketable types**: bills, notes, bonds, TIPS, STRIPS. **Non-marketable** (e.g., **Series I savings bonds**) cannot be resold, so no secondary market.

| Security | Maturity | Interest | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **T-bill** | 4, 13, 26, 52 weeks (≤ 1 yr) | None; sold at **discount**, matures at par | Single-price weekly auctions; quoted on **discount yield** basis |
| **T-note** | 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 years | **Every 6 months** | 10-year is the benchmark quote |
| **T-bond** | 30 years | **Every 6 months** | Longest maturity, most rate-sensitive |
| **TIPS** | Inflation-indexed | Constant coupon on **principal adjusted semiannually by CPI** | Protects against inflation |
| **STRIPS** | Various | Zero coupon, **discount to face** | **No reinvestment risk** |

- Denominations $100 to $5,000,000 for bills and notes. Primary dealers (banks/financial institutions) are the largest bill buyers.
- **STRIPS**: interest and principal of T-notes, T-bonds and TIPS are separated and traded individually. A 10-year note becomes **21 STRIPS** (20 coupons + 1 principal).
- **Treasury receipts**: zero-coupons **created by broker-dealers**, backed by Treasury cash flows, but technically **obligations of the broker-dealer**; lost popularity once the government backed STRIPS.
> **Exam tip** Longer maturity + zero coupon = biggest price swing (30-year STRIP is the most volatile Treasury). Bills = discount, notes/bonds = semiannual coupons.

- **Notes and bonds** are quoted as a **percentage of par in 32nds** (1/32 = 1 *tick*). A point = **$10** per $1,000 bond; one 32nd = **$0.3125**.
  - 95:07 (or 95–07) = 95 7/32% = **$952.19**.
  - Quote layout: ISSUE (coupon, maturity, N = note) | BID | ASK | CHANGE | YIELD. The ask shows **only the 32nds** (e.g., 105.08 bid / 12 ask = 105 8/32 and 105 12/32).
  - **Ask is higher than bid** (buyer pays the ask). Spread = ask − bid; **small spread = liquid**. Change = today’s bid vs prior close bid, in ticks. Yield = return if bought at the ask and held to maturity.
- **Bills** are quoted as a **discount from face**, expressed as an **annual rate on a 360-day year** (*discounted yield basis*).
  - **Bid is HIGHER than ask** because the quoted number is subtracted from face: the buyer wants the bigger discount.
  - **Higher discount yield = lower price.**
> **Exam tip** Notes/bonds: bid < ask. Bills: bid > ask. Spread size is a direct gauge of **liquidity** (and indirectly of volume).

brief.h: Agency securities, MBS, CMOs and ABS
brief.md:
- **Agency securities** are issued by federal agencies and government-sponsored enterprises, **not by the Treasury**. Only **Ginnie Mae (GNMA)** is fully guaranteed (**full faith and credit**); **Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac** carry **implied** backing (now publicly traded corporations, not guaranteed by full faith and credit). Yields are **higher than Treasuries**. On the exam, “agency” may include all three.
- **Mortgage-backed securities (MBS)**: pools of mortgages sliced into $1,000-par, bond-like pieces; **securitization** = pooling. Also called **pass-through certificates**: monthly interest **and a share of principal** pass through to investors, so MBS **pay monthly** and offer good current income. Safe, slightly higher interest than Treasuries and many investment-grade corporates.
- **Prepayment risk** (rates **fall**): homeowners refinance, pools shrink, maturity shortens, like a call: **reinvestment rate risk** (money back early, reinvested lower) and **no price gain** despite falling rates (acts like a short-term security).
- **Extension risk** (rates **rise**): no refinancing, slower prepayments, maturity **lengthens**; prices fall **significantly** (long-term, rate-sensitive) and the investor is **stuck longer**.
- **CMOs**: MBS **structured by broker-dealers** into **tranches** (differing expected maturity, credit quality, prepayment exposure), designed to protect against prepayment/extension risk. Pay interest and principal; price affected by credit quality of the underlying mortgages.
- **ABS**: pools of non-mortgage assets (credit card debt, auto loans, aircraft leases, royalties, movie revenues). Credit quality tracks the quality of the pooled loans/borrowers.
> **Exam tip** Falling rates = prepayment risk. Rising rates = extension risk. MBS are not all full-faith-and-credit; only GNMA is.

- **Issuers**: states, cities, counties, towns, villages, **interstate** and **intrastate authorities**, and US territories (Guam, Samoa, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands). A **municipal advisor** helps the issuer decide what to issue and how to structure it.
- Munis are backed by taxes or revenues; the **secondary market is highly illiquid** (each issue unique) and trades **OTC** through dealers. Many buyers are **buy-and-hold** for tax benefits.
- **GO bonds**: backed by **full faith and credit** and the **full taxing power** of the issuer (plus legislative authority); no specific asset. Fund **non-revenue-producing** projects that benefit all: roads, parks, schools, government buildings.
- Sources: income and sales taxes, license fees, and mostly **ad valorem taxes** (based on value: **property tax** is the most common source). Property tax is on **assessed value, not market value**, and levied **locally only**, not by states.
- **Debt limits** cap outstanding GO principal; debt far below the limit = **safer**. Many new GOs need **voter approval (bond referendum)**.
- GO bonds may be rated similarly to Treasuries and high-grade corporates (power to raise taxes).
> **Exam tip** GO = taxes, free-to-use facilities, referendum, debt limits. Property taxes use **assessed** value.

brief.h: Revenue bonds and short-term municipal notes
brief.md:
- **Revenue bonds**: backed **only by revenue from the financed project** (user fees), e.g., toll road, airport, water/sewer/power system, convention center. Issuers: essential-service entities (transportation, power, sewer, water), **501(c) nonprofits**, private-sector corporations such as **hospitals**.
- Issuer is **not obligated** to pay from any source other than pledged revenues. **No new taxes**, **no voter approval**, **outside legislative debt limits**.
- An entity providing a **free service** (e.g., public school) **cannot** issue revenue bonds.
- Revenue bonds come with a **bond (trust) indenture** and protective covenants. Munis are **not subject to the Trust Indenture Act of 1939**, yet indentures are standard practice.

| Feature | GO | Revenue |
|---|---|---|
| Backing | Taxing authority, full faith and credit | Project/facility revenues |
| Projects | “Free” to public | “Fee for use” |
| Debt/tax limits | Apply | Do not apply |
| Voter approval | Referendum | Not needed |

- **Short-term municipal notes** (generally **one year or less**, high quality, for cash flow):
  - **TAN**: repaid from future **tax receipts**.
  - **RAN**: repaid from **non-tax revenues** (e.g., sales taxes, as the book uses it).
  - **BAN**: interim financing for capital projects, repaid from **proceeds of a later long-term bond issue**.
> **Exam tip** Match the repayment source to the letter: Tax, Revenue, Bond.

brief.h: Municipal tax treatment and tax-equivalent yield
brief.md:
- **Federal**: interest on **public purpose** munis is **exempt**; **capital gains are taxable**. Unless told otherwise, **assume munis pay tax-exempt interest**.
- **State/local**: interest on bonds issued in the investor’s **own state** is generally free of that state’s income tax (and possibly city tax: NYC resident + NYC bond = **triple-tax-free**). An **out-of-state** muni is state-taxable (NY resident, California bond: federal-free, **state-taxable**).
- **US territory** bonds (Guam, Samoa, Puerto Rico, USVI): exempt from federal, state and local tax **anywhere in the US** = triple-tax-free.
- Higher state income tax = more demand for in-state bonds; **no-income-tax states must offer slightly higher yields**.
- **Private-purpose / private activity** bonds (stadiums, private-jet airports) may be **taxable**. **IDR (industrial development revenue) bonds** benefit a private corporation: taxable; backed by **lease payments** from the company, so they follow the **corporation’s credit quality**.
- **AMT**: interest on certain **private activity bonds** is included in the **alternative minimum tax** calculation (higher of regular vs AMT tax is paid). The **official statement front cover** and the **trade confirmation** disclose AMT status.
- **Suitability**: best for **high-bracket** investors; **unsuitable for retirement accounts/pensions** that are already tax-sheltered.
- Issuer benefit: lower coupons, cheaper borrowing.
- **Tax-equivalent yield = tax-free yield ÷ (100% − tax rate)**.
> **Exam tip** The exemption covers *interest*, not capital gains. In-state vs out-of-state is the favourite trap.

brief.h: Tax treatment summary of fixed-income securities
brief.md:
| Issuer | Federal tax on interest | State/local tax on interest |
|---|---|---|
| **US Treasury securities** | Taxable | **Exempt** |
| **Municipal bonds**, in-state buyer | Exempt | Exempt |
| **Municipal bonds**, out-of-state buyer | Exempt | Taxable |
| **Corporate bonds** | Taxable | Taxable |
| **CMOs** and **foreign debt** | Taxable | Taxable |

- The book states most fixed-income (except munis) is taxed by both federal and state/local governments, with **Treasuries** the exception for state/local.
- Unit exam logic: of Treasuries, Ginnie Maes, CMOs and corporates, **only Treasuries** are state/local exempt.
- Retirement accounts and pensions are already sheltered, so tax-free munis add nothing there.
> **Exam tip** Ranking of tax-friendliness: municipal (public purpose) > Treasury > corporate.

- Money market = debt with the **shortest maturities, typically under one year**; near-cash, liquid, low risk (quality varies with issuer). Primarily **institutional**, large denominations; individuals mostly use **money market mutual funds** (treated like “cash” in a brokerage account).
- Eligible: **T-bills**, T-notes/T-bonds **with one year or less left**, negotiable CDs, commercial paper, banker’s acceptances, repos. **No equities** (ADRs, preferred stock). Long-term munis do not belong in a money market fund.
- **Commercial paper (CP)**: negotiable, **unsecured** corporate promissory note for working capital; issued at a **discount**; **maximum 270 days** to be exempt from SEC registration under the ’33 Act.
- **CDs**: bank deposits/notes with fixed maturities; FDIC-insured up to **$250,000 per depositor**; early-redemption penalties.
  - **Non-negotiable** (most retail CDs): cannot be resold, only redeemed at the issuing bank; **not securities**, do not trade in the money market.
  - **Negotiable**: transferable, securities, trade in the secondary market (limited), minimum face value **$100,000**; interest is taxable.
- **Banker’s acceptance (BA)**: short-term negotiable **time draft**, guaranteed by a bank; **borrower and bank both liable**; typically **180 days or less**; traditionally finances **international trade**.
- **Repo**: sale of securities with commitment to **buy back later at a higher price** (the difference is the lender’s interest), like a collateralized short-term loan. The party selling then repurchasing is in the **repo**; the other side is in the **reverse repo**.
- The **Fed** uses them for monetary policy: **repos add** reserves temporarily; **reverse repos drain** reserves.
> **Exam tip** Two ceilings: CP 270 days, BA about 180 days. Non-negotiable CDs are not money market securities.

traps: **Conversion ratio uses par, not market price.** A $1,000 par convertible with a $25 conversion price gives 40 shares even if the bond trades at $800 or $1,300.

**Convertible coupon.** Convertibles pay a **lower** coupon than comparable straight bonds because the investor holds an equity option. They trade like equity and are *more* volatile than other debt when rates are stable.

**Debenture vs secured.** Debenture = unsecured corporate debt (synonyms). Secured types are mortgage, collateral trust and equipment trust. Debentures pay **more** than secured; subordinated debentures pay more still.
**Eurodollar bond vs Eurodollar deposit.** Bond = issued outside the US in dollars (not SEC-registered). Deposit = US dollars held in a foreign bank.
**Bid vs ask: notes/bonds vs bills.** Notes and bonds: ask above bid. Bills are quoted by discount: **bid above ask**, and a higher discount means a lower price.
**T-bill vs T-note vs T-bond.** Bills: ≤ 1 year, discount, no coupons. Notes: 2–10 years, semiannual coupons. Bonds: 30 years, semiannual coupons. None pay annually.
**STRIPS vs Treasury receipts.** STRIPS are the Treasury’s own program (government-backed). Receipts were created by broker-dealers and are obligations of the dealer.
**GNMA vs Fannie/Freddie.** Only GNMA has full faith and credit; Fannie and Freddie are implied backing. The exam may still call all three “agency”.
**Prepayment vs extension risk.** Falling rates cause prepayment (maturity shortens, reinvest lower). Rising rates cause extension (maturity lengthens, price drops sharply).
**MBS vs CMO.** MBS are plain pass-throughs of mortgage pools. CMOs are MBS restructured by broker-dealers into tranches with different maturity/credit/prepayment profiles.
**GO vs revenue.** GO = taxing power, non-revenue projects, voter referendum, debt limits. Revenue = user fees, no referendum, outside debt limits, issuer pays only from pledged revenues.
**Property tax basis.** Ad valorem property taxes use **assessed** value, not market value, and are levied locally, never by the state.
**Muni exemption covers interest only.** Capital gains on a muni are taxable. Out-of-state munis are federally exempt but state-taxable; territory bonds are triple-tax-free everywhere.
**Money market eligibility.** Negotiable CDs, CP, BAs, T-bills yes. Non-negotiable CDs, long-term munis and any equity (ADRs, preferred) no. Only T-notes/T-bonds with ≤ 1 year left qualify.

formulas.name: Conversion ratio
formulas.rule: Conversion ratio = Par value ÷ Conversion price (always par, never the market price). Shares received = ratio × number of bonds.
formulas.example: Conversion price $40 → $1,000 ÷ $40 = **25 shares** per bond (25:1). A holder of 8 bonds receives 8 × 25 = **200 shares**, even if the bonds trade at $850.

formulas.name: Treasury note/bond quote in dollars
formulas.rule: Price = (whole points + 32nds ÷ 32) × $10 per point on $1,000 par. One 32nd = $0.3125. Spread = ask − bid in 32nds.

formulas.name: Tax-equivalent yield
formulas.rule: Tax-equivalent yield = Tax-free yield ÷ (100% − tax rate). Compare it with the taxable yield: higher wins after tax.
formulas.example: Muni 4.5% for an investor in the 25% bracket: 4.5% ÷ 0.75 = **6.00%**. A taxable bond yielding 6.5% beats the muni; one yielding 5.5% does not.

formulas.name: Number of STRIPS from a coupon security
formulas.rule: STRIPS = (number of semiannual coupons) + 1 principal strip = (years × 2) + 1.

formulas.name: Rate-change risk map for MBS/CMO
formulas.rule: Rates ↓ → prepayments ↑ → maturity shortens → **prepayment risk** (reinvestment risk, limited price gain). Rates ↑ → prepayments ↓ → maturity lengthens → **extension risk** (large price drop).
formulas.example: Mortgage rates fall 1.5 points: homeowners refinance, pool principal returns early, investor reinvests at lower yields → **prepayment risk**.

formulas.name: GO vs revenue decision rule
formulas.rule: Free public use + general benefit → **GO** (taxes, referendum, debt limits). Facility charges fees → **revenue** (pledged revenues, indenture, no referendum, outside debt limits). Free-service entity cannot issue revenue bonds.
formulas.example: A new toll bridge funded by tolls → **revenue bond**. A new public library funded by property taxes → **GO bond**.

glossary.d: Debt issued by a commercial or industrial company to raise expansion money, generally with maturities of at least 10 years and fully taxable interest.
Law requiring corporate debt issues above $50 million to have a written indenture with an independent trustee.
The written agreement between issuer and trustee containing the bondholders’ protective covenants.
A promise by the issuer in the indenture that protects bondholders, e.g., maintain insurance or not sell key assets.
An independent party, typically a large bank, that enforces the indenture on behalf of bondholders.
Corporate bond secured by real estate or other real property.
Corporate bond secured by financial assets owned by the issuer, such as stocks or bonds.
Corporate debt secured by physical equipment such as aircraft, trucks and trains.
Unsecured corporate debt backed only by the issuer’s good faith; same as unsecured corporate debt.
Unsecured debt ranking below senior debt in bankruptcy, so it pays higher interest.
The Bankruptcy Code order of repayment: secured, unsecured, subordinated/convertible, preferred, common.
Corporate bond that the holder may convert into a fixed number of the issuer’s common shares.
The stated price per share at which a convertible bond can be exchanged for common stock.
Number of common shares received per bond, equal to par divided by the conversion price.
The market value at which an investor is indifferent between holding the convertible bond and converting to stock.
A bond issued outside the US but denominated in US dollars and not registered with the SEC.
US dollars held in a bank outside the United States.
Difference between the price a buyer bids and a seller asks; narrow means liquid.
Treasury security maturing in one year or less, sold at a discount and paying par at maturity.
Treasury security with 2- to 10-year maturity paying interest every six months.
Longest Treasury security, currently 30 years, paying semiannual interest.
Treasury inflation-protected securities whose principal is adjusted semiannually by the CPI while the coupon rate stays constant.
Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal Securities: zero-coupon Treasuries created by separating coupons and principal.
Zero-coupon security created by a broker-dealer from Treasury cash flows and technically an obligation of that dealer.
Quoting method for T-bills as an annual discount rate on a 360-day year.
Debt issued by federal agencies or GSEs, not by the Treasury, generally yielding more than Treasuries.
Government agency whose securities carry the full faith and credit of the US government.
Publicly traded corporations (former GSEs) whose securities carry implied, not explicit, government backing.
Bond-like security representing a pool of mortgages that passes monthly interest and principal to investors.
Risk that falling rates cause early mortgage repayments, shortening maturity and forcing reinvestment at lower rates.
Risk that rising rates slow prepayments, lengthening an MBS and causing a large price decline.
MBS structured by broker-dealers into tranches with different maturity, credit and prepayment characteristics.
Security backed by a pool of non-mortgage assets such as auto loans, credit card debt or royalties.
Municipal bond backed by the issuer’s full faith, credit and taxing power, used for non-revenue-producing projects.
Tax based on value, such as property tax, the most common source for repaying GO bonds.
Municipal bond repaid solely from revenues of the financed project, such as tolls or user fees.
Short-term municipal notes repaid, respectively, from future tax receipts, non-tax revenues, and later long-term bond proceeds.
Municipal bond benefiting the community at large, whose interest is exempt from federal income tax.
Municipal bond benefiting private users, such as stadiums or IDRs, that may be taxable and can trigger AMT.
Municipal bond issued for a private corporation, backed by its lease payments, and taxable.
Separate tax computation that includes private activity bond interest; the higher of AMT or regular tax is owed.
Municipal bond’s primary disclosure document; its front cover indicates AMT status.
Interest exempt from federal, state and local income tax, e.g., territory bonds or in-state, in-city munis.
Taxable yield needed to match a tax-free yield: tax-free yield divided by (100% minus tax rate).
Market for short-term, liquid, low-risk debt generally maturing in a year or less.
Unsecured negotiable corporate promissory note, issued at a discount with maturity up to 270 days.
Bank CD that can be transferred to other investors, with a $100,000 minimum face value.
Retail bank CD that cannot be resold and is not a money market security.
Short-term negotiable time draft guaranteed by a bank, used to finance international trade.
Sale of securities with an agreement to buy them back later at a higher price, functioning as a collateralized loan.

cards.f: Typical maturity of a corporate bond vs note vs commercial paper
cards.b: Bond: at least **10 years**. Note: medium-term. Commercial paper: **no more than 270 days**.
**Fully taxable** as ordinary income at federal, state and local level.

cards.f: What does the Trust Indenture Act of 1939 require?
cards.b: Corporate debt issues of **more than $50 million** need a written trust indenture with an independent trustee.
An issuer promise in the indenture that **protects bondholders** (file SEC reports, pay taxes, keep insurance, no sale of key assets, maintain credit profile).
Acts for bondholders; typically a large **bank**; on default may **seize and sell assets** to repay holders.
**Real estate** or other real property.

cards.f: Collateral trust bond is secured by...
cards.b: **Financial assets** the issuer owns (stocks, bonds, other securities).

cards.f: Equipment trust obligation is secured by...
cards.b: **Physical equipment**: airplanes, trucks, trains.
**Unsecured** corporate debt, backed by good faith only; pays more than secured debt.

cards.f: Why does subordinated debt pay more interest?
cards.b: Lower bankruptcy priority than senior debt = **greater risk**, so higher yield.

cards.f: Order of repayment in a corporate bankruptcy
cards.b: **Secured → unsecured/general creditors → subordinated and convertible → preferred → common.**
Convertible pays a **lower coupon**.
**Lower fixed borrowing cost** and **no immediate dilution** of common shares.
More like **equities** than bonds; with stable rates, more volatile than other debt because they follow the **underlying stock**.
**Par value ÷ conversion price**; always based on par, not market price.
Value at which the investor is **indifferent** between the bond and the shares; no gain or loss at conversion.
Issued **outside the US**, denominated in **US dollars**, not SEC-registered.
**US dollars held in a bank abroad**.

cards.f: What drives liquidity differences between two corporate bonds?
cards.b: Mainly **credit rating**, more than coupon or maturity.
**Full faith and credit**; interest **federally taxable, state/local exempt**.
**Bills, notes, bonds, TIPS, STRIPS.**
**4, 13, 26 and 52 weeks** (one year or less).

cards.f: How does a T-bill pay interest?
cards.b: No coupons: sold at a **discount**, matures at **par**; difference is the interest.
**2, 3, 5, 7, 10 years**; interest **every six months**.

cards.f: Benchmark of the US government bond market
cards.b: The **10-year Treasury note**.
**30 years**, interest every six months.

cards.f: 95:07 on a T-note equals how many dollars?

cards.b: Principal adjusted **semiannually by CPI**; coupon rate constant, so interest rises with inflation.
Separately traded interest and principal pieces of T-notes, T-bonds and TIPS; effectively **zero-coupon** Treasuries.

cards.f: How many STRIPS from a 10-year T-note?
cards.b: **21** (20 interest payments + 1 principal).
**None**: no coupons to reinvest.
Zero-coupons **structured by broker-dealers**, backed by Treasury cash flows, but obligations of the dealer.
**Ask is higher** than bid; spread = ask − bid; small spread = liquid.
As a **discount from face**, annual rate on a **360-day year** (discounted yield basis).
**Bid is higher than ask**; higher discount yield = **lower price**.

cards.f: Which agency debt has full faith and credit backing?
cards.b: **GNMA (Ginnie Mae)** only. Fannie and Freddie are implied.

cards.f: How often do MBS pay and what?
cards.b: **Monthly** interest plus a share of principal (pass-through).
When rates **fall**: homeowners refinance, maturity shortens, money is reinvested at **lower** rates.
**No meaningful increase**: the MBS acts like a short-term security.
When rates **rise**: no refinancing, maturity **lengthens**, price falls significantly.
MBS **structured by broker-dealers** into **tranches** (different maturity, credit, prepayment exposure).
ABS pool **non-mortgage** assets (auto loans, credit cards, leases, royalties); credit quality follows the pooled assets.
**Full faith and credit** and **taxing power** of the issuer.
**Non-revenue-producing** projects: roads, parks, schools, government buildings.
**Ad valorem property tax**, based on **assessed** value, levied **locally** only.

**Voter approval** required for many new GO issues; not needed for revenue bonds.
Only the **revenue of the financed facility** (fees, tolls, charges).
Transportation, power, sewer, water systems; **501(c)** nonprofits; private corporations such as hospitals.

cards.f: Can a public school issue revenue bonds?
cards.b: **No**: a free service has no revenue source beyond taxes.
Not backed by taxes, so can be issued **outside legislative debt limits**.

cards.f: Munis and the Trust Indenture Act
cards.b: Munis are **not subject** to it, but revenue bond **indentures are standard**.
Short-term munis repaid from **taxes** / **non-tax revenues** / **later bond proceeds**.

cards.f: Federal tax on public purpose muni interest vs capital gains
cards.b: Interest **exempt**; capital gains **taxable**.

cards.f: Who benefits most from tax-free munis?
cards.b: Investors in **high tax brackets**; unsuitable for retirement accounts/pensions.

cards.f: NY resident buys NY muni vs California muni
cards.b: NY bond: free of federal and NY state tax. California bond: free federally, **state-taxable**.
Exempt from federal, state and local tax: US **territory** bonds anywhere; in-city bond for local residents.

cards.f: Why might a muni be taxable?
cards.b: **Private-purpose / private activity** use, e.g., stadiums, private airports, **IDR** bonds.
**Lease payments** from the corporation; credit quality follows the company.
Interest on certain **private activity bonds** is included in the AMT; shown on the official statement cover and trade confirmation.
**Tax-free yield ÷ (100% − tax rate)**. 5% at 35% = **7.69%**.
Typically **one year or less**; near-cash and liquid.

cards.f: Which securities cannot be in the money market?
cards.b: **Equities** such as ADRs or preferred stock.
Unsecured corporate promissory note at a discount; max **270 days** for ’33 Act registration exemption.
Negotiable: transferable, security, **$100,000 minimum**. Non-negotiable: cannot be resold, not a security.
**$250,000** per depositor.
Time draft guaranteed by a bank, typically **180 days or less**, finances **international trade**.
Repo: sell securities and agree to **buy back higher**. Reverse repo: the buyer’s side. Repos add reserves; reverse repos drain them.

questions.q: The Trust Indenture Act of 1939 requires a written trust indenture with an independent trustee for corporate debt issues of what size?
o: Any corporate issue, regardless of size
Only issues of $500 million or more
w: Correct: corporate issues above $50 million must have a trust indenture and an independent trustee for the bondholders.
Wrong: the Act has a size threshold, so small issues are not automatically covered by it.
Wrong: this figure is ten times too low compared with the threshold in the Act.
Wrong: this threshold is ten times too high; the Act already applies once an issue exceeds $50 million.

questions.q: Which of the following is another name for unsecured corporate debt?
w: Wrong: a mortgage bond is secured by real estate or other real property, so it is not unsecured.
Correct: a debenture is backed only by the issuer’s good faith and credit, with no specific collateral.
Wrong: equipment trust obligations are secured by physical equipment such as aircraft, trucks and trains.
Wrong: collateral trust bonds are secured by financial assets such as stocks or bonds owned by the issuer.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical protective covenant in a corporate trust indenture?
o: Guarantee that the issuer’s stock price will rise
w: Wrong: maintaining insurance is a classic covenant that protects the value of the issuer’s assets for bondholders.
Wrong: paying taxes is a standard covenant, since unpaid taxes could threaten the issuer’s assets.
Correct: an issuer cannot promise a stock price outcome; covenants are controllable promises like filings, taxes and insurance.
Wrong: submitting SEC filings is a typical covenant that keeps bondholders informed about the issuer.

questions.q: Brightwater Corp. files for bankruptcy and liquidates. Four investors each hold a different security of the company. Which investor is paid first?
o: Holder of a senior unsecured debenture
w: Wrong: preferred stockholders rank behind all bondholders and are paid only after debt is satisfied.
Wrong: subordinated debt is junior to senior unsecured debt, so it is repaid later in the waterfall.
Wrong: common stockholders are last in the liquidation order and receive only what remains.
Correct: senior unsecured creditors are paid before subordinated debt, preferred stock and common stock.

questions.q: Equipment trust obligations are secured by which of the following?
o: Stocks and bonds owned by the issuer
Only the issuer’s good faith and credit
w: Correct: equipment trust obligations are backed by physical assets such as aircraft, trucks and railcars.
Wrong: real estate collateral describes a mortgage bond, not an equipment trust obligation.
Wrong: financial assets owned by the issuer secure collateral trust bonds.
Wrong: backing by good faith alone describes an unsecured debenture.

questions.q: A corporation has two bonds outstanding with the same maturity: a mortgage bond and a subordinated debenture. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The mortgage bond will pay the higher yield because it is backed by real estate
The subordinated debenture will generally pay the higher yield because it ranks lower in liquidation
Both pay the same yield because they have the same issuer
The subordinated debenture has the higher priority because it is unsecured
w: Wrong: collateral lowers risk, so the secured mortgage bond generally pays less than junior debt.
Correct: lower liquidation priority means greater risk, which investors are paid for with a higher yield.
Wrong: same issuer does not mean same yield; the rank in the capital structure changes the risk.
Wrong: secured debt is paid first and subordinated debt ranks below unsecured senior debt.

questions.q: In a corporate bankruptcy, which of the following are paid before preferred stockholders? I. Secured bondholders II. Subordinated debenture holders III. Convertible bondholders IV. Common stockholders
w: Wrong: this leaves out convertible bondholders, who are creditors that rank with subordinated debt, ahead of preferred stock.
Wrong: secured bondholders are also paid ahead of preferred stock, indeed ahead of everyone.
Correct: all bondholders, secured, subordinated and convertible, rank ahead of preferred; common stock ranks last.
Wrong: common stockholders are paid after preferred stockholders, not before.

questions.q: A convertible bond with a $1,000 par value has a conversion price of $50 per share. What is its conversion ratio?
w: Wrong: this divides $500 by the price; the ratio is based on the $1,000 par value.
Wrong: 50 is the conversion price itself, not the number of shares received for the bond.
Wrong: dividing by $40 would give 25; the stated conversion price is $50.
Correct: conversion ratio = par ÷ conversion price = $1,000 ÷ $50 = 20 shares per bond.

questions.q: A convertible bond has a conversion price of $12.50 and currently trades at $900. An investor holds 10 of these bonds and converts them all. How many common shares does she receive?
w: Correct: ratio = $1,000 ÷ $12.50 = 80 shares per bond; 80 × 10 bonds = 800 shares.
Wrong: this wrongly uses the $900 market price ($900 ÷ $12.50 = 72 per bond); the ratio always uses par.
Wrong: this is the ratio for a single bond; she is converting ten bonds.
Wrong: this multiplies by 100 instead of 10; ten bonds at 80 shares each give 800.

questions.q: A $1,000 par convertible bond has a conversion price of $40 and trades at $1,100. The issuer’s common stock is trading at $48. What is the market value of the shares received if one bond is converted?
w: Wrong: $1,100 is the bond’s market price, not the value of the shares received on conversion.
Correct: ratio = $1,000 ÷ $40 = 25 shares; 25 × $48 = $1,200 of stock.
Wrong: $1,000 is par; the shares are valued at the current stock price, not at par.
Wrong: this multiplies the stock price by the conversion price ($48 × $40) instead of by the 25 shares.

questions.q: Compared with a non-convertible bond of the same issuer and maturity, a convertible bond typically has which of the following?
o: A guaranteed price floor at par
w: Wrong: convertibles rank with subordinated debt, below secured and senior unsecured debt.
Wrong: the conversion feature has value to the investor, so the issuer can offer a lower, not higher, coupon.
Correct: investors accept a lower coupon in exchange for the option to convert into common stock.
Wrong: the price can fall to the level where its yield matches a non-convertible bond, not necessarily par.

questions.q: Interest rates have been stable for a year while an issuer’s common stock has risen sharply. Compared with the issuer’s straight (non-convertible) bonds, its convertible bond will most likely:
o: Behave exactly like its preferred stock
Remain flat because the coupon is fixed
Fall in price because yields are stable
Rise with the stock and show more price volatility
w: Wrong: the bond’s price is tied to the common stock through conversion, not to preferred stock.
Wrong: a fixed coupon does not freeze the price; the conversion feature links the bond to the stock.
Wrong: stable rates give no reason for the price to fall, and the rising stock pushes the convertible up.
Correct: with stable rates the convertible follows the underlying stock, making it more volatile than other debt.

questions.q: Which is a reason an issuer may sell convertible bonds rather than additional common stock?
o: It avoids immediate dilution of existing common shares and lowers fixed borrowing costs
Convertible holders have no claim on assets in bankruptcy
Interest on convertibles is not owed until conversion occurs
The conversion price must always equal par value
w: Correct: debt does not add shares at issuance, and the lower coupon reduces the fixed cost of borrowing.
Wrong: convertible holders are creditors and do have a claim, ranking with subordinated debt.
Wrong: convertibles pay interest like any other bond; the conversion option does not defer coupons.
Wrong: the conversion price is set in the indenture and the ratio is par divided by that price, not equal to par.

questions.q: A bond issued outside the United States, denominated in US dollars and not registered with the SEC is called a:
w: Wrong: a Eurodollar deposit is a dollar balance held at a bank abroad, not a bond.
Correct: Eurodollar bonds are issued and traded outside the US but denominated in US dollars.
Wrong: Treasury receipts are zero-coupons created by broker-dealers from Treasury cash flows.
Wrong: a collateral trust bond is secured by financial assets and has nothing to do with the place of issue.

questions.q: A client keeps US dollars in an account at a bank in Switzerland. How is this holding best described?
w: Wrong: a bond is a debt security; the client simply holds a bank balance.
Wrong: Treasury receipts are broker-dealer zero-coupon securities, unrelated to a bank account.
Correct: US dollars held in a bank outside the US are Eurodollar deposits.
Wrong: the balance is denominated in US dollars, not a foreign currency, and it is not a bond.

questions.q: Two corporate bonds trade in the secondary market. Which factor would most likely explain a difference in their liquidity?
o: A difference in the day of the week they were issued
w: Wrong: the day of issue has no bearing on secondary-market liquidity.
Wrong: coupon differences affect price and yield but are less important for liquidity than credit rating.
Wrong: maturity affects rate sensitivity, yet the book names credit rating as the bigger liquidity driver.
Correct: credit quality affects demand and dealer willingness to hold the bond more than coupon or maturity do.

questions.q: All of the following are true of Eurodollar bonds EXCEPT:
o: They are registered with the SEC
They are denominated in US dollars
They are issued outside the United States
They trade outside the United States
w: Correct: Eurodollar bonds are not registered with the SEC, so this statement is the false one.
Wrong: this is true; the dollar denomination is what defines the instrument.
Wrong: this is true; Eurodollar bonds are issued outside the US, for example in Argentina.
Wrong: this is true; they are issued and trade outside the United States.

questions.q: Interest paid on a corporate bond is generally:
o: Exempt from state and local tax but taxable federally
Taxable as ordinary income at the federal, state and local levels
Exempt from federal tax but taxable by the state
Taxed only when the bond is sold
w: Wrong: that treatment describes US Treasury securities, not corporate bonds.
Correct: corporate interest has no exemption and is taxed as ordinary income at every level.
Wrong: federal exemption is the feature of public purpose municipal bonds.
Wrong: interest is taxed as received, not only when the bond is sold.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a maturity at which Treasury bills are issued?
w: Wrong: a four-week bill is one of the standard T-bill maturities.
Wrong: 26 weeks is a standard bill maturity.
Correct: two years is a T-note maturity; bills mature in one year or less.
Wrong: 52 weeks, one year, is the longest T-bill maturity.

questions.q: How often do Treasury notes and Treasury bonds pay interest?
w: Wrong: monthly payments are characteristic of mortgage-backed securities.
Wrong: paying only at maturity describes T-bills and zero-coupon securities such as STRIPS.
Wrong: annual payment is a common trap; Treasury coupons are paid twice a year.
Correct: T-notes and T-bonds pay interest semiannually.

questions.q: A Treasury note is quoted at an ask of 98.16. Assuming $1,000 par, what price in dollars will a buyer pay?
w: Wrong: the digits after the decimal are 32nds, not hundredths of a dollar, so 16 is not 16 tenths.
Wrong: this rounds incorrectly; 16/32 is exactly one half point, which is $5.
Wrong: this treats .16 as cents per bond; the quote is in 32nds of a point.

questions.q: A Treasury bond is quoted at an ask of 101.08. Assuming $1,000 par, what is the price in dollars?
w: Wrong: this reads 08 as hundredths; the figure after the decimal is in 32nds.
Wrong: this ignores the 8/32 entirely and treats 8 as dollars below par.
Wrong: this adds eight full dollars instead of 8/32 of a point.

questions.q: A dealer quotes a Treasury bond at 99.04 bid and 99.08 ask. What is the spread, in dollars, per $1,000 bond? (One 32nd equals $0.3125.)
w: Wrong: this treats the four ticks as 40 cents; each tick is $0.3125, not ten cents.
Wrong: this treats each tick as a whole dollar, which overstates the spread by more than three times.
Correct: the spread is 8/32 − 4/32 = 4 ticks; 4 × $0.3125 = $1.25 per bond.
Wrong: this multiplies by 10 once too often; four ticks do not equal a full point and a quarter.

questions.q: Which statement about Treasury bill quotations is correct?
o: Quotes are based on a 365-day coupon yield
The ask is higher than the bid, as with Treasury bonds
Quotes are expressed as a percentage of par in 32nds
The bid is higher than the ask because the discount is subtracted from face value
w: Wrong: bills use a discounted yield basis on a 360-day year.
Wrong: that ordering applies to notes and bonds, which are quoted by price rather than discount.
Wrong: 32nds are used for notes and bonds, while bills are quoted by annualized discount.
Correct: bills are quoted by discount yield, so the buyer’s bid is a bigger discount than the seller’s ask.

questions.q: Imani wants a newly issued Treasury security that pays a fixed coupon every six months and matures in seven years. Which security fits?
w: Correct: notes are issued with 2, 3, 5, 7 or 10-year maturities and pay semiannual interest.
Wrong: bills mature in one year or less and pay no coupons.
Wrong: Treasury bonds are currently issued with a 30-year maturity.
Wrong: STRIPS are zero-coupon securities and pay no semiannual interest.

questions.q: A 5-year Treasury note is stripped into separate securities, one for each interest payment and one for the principal. How many STRIPS result?
w: Wrong: five would be annual coupons only, but Treasury notes pay twice a year and the principal needs its own strip.
Correct: 5 years × 2 = 10 coupon strips + 1 principal strip = 11 STRIPS.
Wrong: ten covers the semiannual coupons but omits the principal strip.
Wrong: 21 is the figure for a 10-year note, not a 5-year note.

questions.q: What is a key advantage of a Treasury STRIP compared with a coupon-paying Treasury bond of similar maturity?
w: Wrong: zero-coupon, long-term securities are actually more sensitive to rate changes.
Wrong: STRIPS provide no current income, since they are zero-coupon securities.
Correct: STRIPS pay no coupons, so there are no payments to be reinvested at lower rates.
Wrong: Treasury securities carry the government’s backing, not indenture covenants.

questions.q: Treasury receipts differ from Treasury STRIPS because receipts are:
o: Direct obligations of the US Treasury
Technically obligations of the broker-dealer that created them
w: Wrong: receipts are zero-coupon bonds, like STRIPS.
Wrong: that describes STRIPS, which are part of the Treasury’s own program.
Wrong: receipts can trade; non-marketable securities such as Series I savings bonds cannot.
Correct: receipts are structured by broker-dealers and backed by Treasury cash flows but are the dealer’s obligation.

questions.q: The principal of Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS) is adjusted semiannually based on which of the following?
w: Correct: TIPS principal moves with the CPI, so a constant coupon pays more interest as principal rises.
Wrong: Treasury yields are market-driven and do not set TIPS principal adjustments.
Wrong: the federal funds rate is a monetary policy rate, not the TIPS index.
Wrong: Treasuries are not adjusted for credit ratings; they carry full faith and credit.

questions.q: Which of the following Treasury securities would be expected to have the greatest price sensitivity to a change in interest rates?
o: A 30-year Treasury bond paying a coupon
w: Wrong: a short-maturity bill has the least sensitivity to rate changes.
Correct: long maturity combined with no coupons makes a STRIP the most volatile Treasury.
Wrong: the coupons paid on the bond return some value early, making it less sensitive than a zero of the same maturity.
Wrong: a five-year note has a much shorter maturity, so its price moves less.

questions.q: Interest earned on US Treasury securities is:
o: Taxable at federal, state and local levels
Exempt from federal tax but taxable by the state
Taxable federally but exempt from state and local income tax
Fully exempt from all income taxes
w: Wrong: that is how corporate bond interest is taxed, without the Treasury state exemption.
Wrong: this reverses the actual treatment.
Correct: Treasury interest is federally taxable and exempt from state and local income tax.
Wrong: Treasury interest is subject to federal tax.

questions.q: Which of the following pay interest that is exempt from state and local income tax? I. Treasury note II. Corporate bond III. Foreign debt security IV. CMO
w: Wrong: foreign debt and CMOs are taxable by state and local authorities; only the Treasury is exempt.
Wrong: corporate bond interest is fully taxable at state and local levels.
Wrong: neither corporate bonds nor foreign debt securities receive a state and local exemption.
Correct: of these, only Treasury interest is exempt from state and local tax.

questions.q: Which issuer’s securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the US government?
w: Correct: GNMA is a government agency whose securities carry explicit full faith and credit backing.
Wrong: Freddie Mac also carries only implied backing.
Wrong: Fannie Mae carries only implied government backing.
Wrong: private corporations have no government guarantee.

questions.q: Mortgage rates fall sharply. What is the main risk to a holder of a mortgage pass-through certificate?
o: Prepayment risk, with principal returned early and reinvested at lower rates
A large price gain as the average life rises
No risk, since the underlying mortgages are guaranteed
w: Wrong: extension risk arises when rates rise and prepayments slow.
Correct: falling rates trigger refinancing, shortening the life of the pool and forcing reinvestment at lower yields.
Wrong: the average life shortens, not rises, and the price does not benefit much because it behaves like a short-term security.
Wrong: pass-through holders still face prepayment risk regardless of credit support.

questions.q: Mortgage rates rise significantly. Which outcome is most likely for a holder of a mortgage pass-through security?
o: The security’s maturity shortens and its price rises
Prepayments rise and the investor must reinvest at higher rates
Prepayments slow, the maturity extends and the price falls significantly
Monthly payments stop until rates fall
w: Wrong: maturity extends, not shortens, and prices of long-term securities fall.
Wrong: prepayments fall when rates rise because there is no incentive to refinance.
Correct: borrowers keep low-rate mortgages longer, so the security lengthens and its price drops sharply.
Wrong: borrowers keep making monthly payments, which continue to pass through.

questions.q: A CMO differs from a basic mortgage pass-through security because a CMO:
o: Is a direct obligation of the US Treasury
Is backed by credit card receivables
Is divided by broker-dealers into tranches with different maturity and risk profiles
w: Wrong: CMOs are structured by broker-dealers and are not Treasury obligations.
Wrong: credit card receivables back ABS, not CMOs.
Wrong: CMOs pay both interest and principal.
Correct: CMOs are structured into tranches to address prepayment and extension risk.

questions.q: An asset-backed security may be backed by all of the following EXCEPT:
o: The taxing power of a municipality
w: Correct: taxing power backs general obligation municipal bonds, not asset-backed securities.
Wrong: credit card debt is a classic ABS collateral pool.
Wrong: aircraft leases are an example of more complex cash flows used for ABS.
Wrong: auto loans are a common ABS asset pool.

questions.q: How do mortgage-backed pass-through securities typically pay investors?
o: Monthly, with interest and a share of principal
Only at maturity, with a lump sum
w: Wrong: semiannual interest-only payments describe Treasury notes and bonds.
Correct: homeowners’ monthly payments of interest and principal are passed through to investors.
Wrong: MBS investors receive payments every month and also receive principal.
Wrong: a single lump sum at maturity describes zero-coupon securities.

questions.q: A Treasury note quote shows a bid of 105.08 and an ask of 12. What does the ask represent?
w: Wrong: the 105 whole points still apply, so the price is far above 12/32 of par.
Wrong: this treats 12 as hundredths; the digits are 32nds.
Correct: the ask shows only the 32nds, 105 and 12/32, which is 105.375% of par, or $1,053.75.
Wrong: the ask is expressed in 32nds of a point, not basis points.

questions.q: Series I savings bonds issued by the Treasury are best described as:
o: Marketable securities that trade in the secondary market
Non-marketable securities that cannot be resold
w: Wrong: 32nd quotations are used for marketable T-notes and T-bonds.
Wrong: marketable Treasuries are bills, notes, bonds, TIPS and STRIPS.
Wrong: STRIPS are marketable and are created by separating interest and principal.
Correct: non-marketable government securities cannot be resold and have no secondary market.

questions.q: General obligation municipal bonds are backed by which of the following?
o: The full faith, credit and taxing power of the issuer
A pledge of the issuer’s equipment
A guarantee from the US Treasury
w: Correct: GO bonds rely on the issuer’s full faith and credit, mainly its power to tax.
Wrong: facility revenue backs revenue bonds, not GOs.
Wrong: GO bonds are not backed by specific assets or equipment.
Wrong: municipal bonds are not guaranteed by the US Treasury.

questions.q: Principal and interest on a revenue bond are paid from which source?
o: The general taxing power of the municipality
Income generated by the financed project
w: Wrong: general taxing power backs GO bonds.
Correct: revenue bonds are repaid from the user fees and income of the project they finance.
Wrong: revenue bonds do not rely on federal funding.
Wrong: property taxes are a typical GO source, not a source for revenue bonds.

questions.q: A town wants to finance a new public library that charges no fees. Which type of bond is most appropriate?
w: Wrong: a free facility generates no revenue to repay a revenue bond.
Wrong: IDR bonds benefit a private corporation and are taxable.
Correct: non-revenue-producing community projects are financed with GO bonds backed by taxes.
Wrong: a BAN is short-term interim financing, not the long-term financing for the library.

questions.q: A county issues bonds to build a toll bridge, to be repaid solely from toll collections. Which statement is true?
o: The issue typically requires voter approval through a bond referendum
The bonds are subject to the Trust Indenture Act of 1939
The bonds are backed by the county’s full taxing power
The bonds can be issued outside the county’s legislative debt limits
w: Wrong: referendums apply to GO bonds, not to revenue bonds.
Wrong: municipal issues are not subject to the Act, even though indentures are standard.
Wrong: a revenue bond is repaid only from pledged revenues, not by general taxes.
Correct: because they are not backed by taxes, revenue bonds can be issued outside legislative debt limits.

questions.q: All of the following are typical of revenue bonds EXCEPT:
o: Backing by the issuer’s full taxing power
A bond indenture with protective covenants
w: Correct: full taxing power backs GO bonds; revenue bond issuers are not obligated beyond pledged revenues.
Wrong: the indenture is an agreement between the issuer and a trustee.
Wrong: pledged project revenues are the defining source of repayment.
Wrong: revenue bonds are generally issued with an indenture containing protective covenants.

questions.q: Property taxes used to repay GO bonds are computed on a property’s:
w: Wrong: the assessed value, not the market value, is used to compute the tax.
Correct: property taxes are based on assessed value, which can differ from market value.
Wrong: the purchase price is not the basis for the tax computation.
Wrong: replacement cost is not the tax base.

questions.q: Which GO issuer would generally be viewed as offering investors the greatest safety?
o: One whose debt is at its debt limit
One whose outstanding debt is far below its debt limit
One that issues only revenue bonds
w: Wrong: GO safety depends on taxing authority, which this issuer lacks.
Wrong: an issuer at its limit has no flexibility and is viewed as riskier.
Correct: ample room under the debt limit signals capacity to borrow and repay.
Wrong: an issuer of only revenue bonds is not a GO issuer, and revenue bonds rely on facility income.

questions.q: Which of the following can issue revenue bonds? I. An airport authority II. A public school district providing free education III. A private hospital IV. A municipal water system
w: Wrong: this omits private hospitals, which are among the typical private-sector revenue bond issuers.
Wrong: a free public school has no revenue source other than tax dollars or government funding.
Wrong: this includes the school district and omits the airport and water system.
Correct: airports, hospitals and water systems generate revenue; a free-service school cannot issue revenue bonds.

questions.q: A city needs interim funding for a capital project until it can sell long-term bonds next year. Which instrument is it most likely to issue?
w: Correct: BANs are repaid from the proceeds of the later long-term bond issue.
Wrong: TANs are repaid from future tax receipts, not from bond proceeds.
Wrong: RANs are repaid from non-tax revenues the municipality expects to receive.
Wrong: commercial paper is issued by corporations, not municipalities.

questions.q: A county needs cash now and expects ad valorem tax receipts in six months. Which short-term obligation fits?
w: Wrong: BANs are repaid from long-term bond proceeds, not tax receipts.
Correct: a TAN is issued in anticipation of future tax receipts and repaid from them.
Wrong: BAs are bank-guaranteed time drafts used in trade finance.
Wrong: CDs are bank instruments, not municipal cash-flow notes.

questions.q: A New York State resident buys a public purpose bond issued by a New York municipality. The interest is:
o: Taxable federally but exempt from New York tax
Exempt from federal tax but taxable by New York State
Exempt from federal and New York State income tax
w: Wrong: federal exemption applies to public purpose municipal interest.
Wrong: the state exemption applies to in-state residents who buy their own state’s bonds.
Correct: public purpose muni interest is federally exempt, and the in-state purchaser also avoids state tax.
Wrong: public purpose bonds are not taxed at the federal level.

questions.q: An Ohio resident purchases a Puerto Rico public purpose bond. How is the interest taxed?
o: Exempt from federal, state and local tax
w: Wrong: this ignores the tax exemption for public purpose and territory bonds.
Wrong: territory bond interest is also exempt from state and local tax, so the exemption goes further.
Wrong: federal exemption applies as well, and for territories the state exemption holds regardless of residence.
Correct: territory bonds are triple-tax-free anywhere in the US.

questions.q: An investor owns $25,000 par of a 4% public purpose municipal bond. What is the annual federally tax-exempt interest?
w: Correct: $25,000 × 4% = $1,000 per year, exempt from federal income tax.
Wrong: $250 is 1% of par, not 4%.
Wrong: $100 is only 4% of $2,500.
Wrong: $4,000 would be 16% of $25,000.

questions.q: An investor in the 25% tax bracket owns a 4.5% tax-free municipal bond. What is the tax-equivalent yield?
w: Wrong: this multiplies 4.5% by 1.25, which is not the formula.
Wrong: this multiplies 4.5% by 1.5 for no valid reason.
Wrong: this multiplies by 0.75, which gives the after-tax yield on a taxable bond, not the tax-equivalent yield.

questions.q: An investor in the 40% bracket compares a 3.6% municipal bond with a 5.5% corporate bond of similar quality. Which statement is correct?
o: The municipal bond is better; its tax-equivalent yield is 5.04%
The corporate bond is better because 5.5% exceeds 3.6%
The municipal bond is better; its tax-equivalent yield is 6.00%
w: Wrong: the conclusion is right but 5.04% comes from multiplying by 1.4 instead of dividing by 0.6.
Wrong: comparing nominal yields ignores the tax; the corporate yield is only 3.3% after tax.
Correct: 3.6% ÷ 0.60 = 6.00%, above 5.5%; the corporate nets 5.5% × 0.60 = 3.3%, below 3.6%.
Wrong: the two are not equal; 6.00% versus 5.5% shows the muni is better.

questions.q: An investor in the 30% bracket compares a 4.5% tax-free municipal bond with a 7% taxable corporate bond. Which gives the higher after-tax return?
o: The municipal bond: 4.50% versus 2.10% for the corporate
The municipal bond, since tax-free always wins
The corporate bond: 4.90% after tax versus 4.50%
w: Wrong: after tax the two returns are 4.90% and 4.50%, not equal.
Wrong: 2.10% is the tax paid on the corporate interest, not what remains after tax.
Wrong: tax-free does not always win; the yield difference and the bracket matter.
Correct: corporate after tax = 7% × (1 − 0.30) = 4.90%, which beats the tax-free 4.50% (tax-equivalent yield 6.43%).

questions.q: An industrial development revenue (IDR) bond is best described as:
o: Backed by lease payments from a private corporation, so its credit follows the corporation
A GO bond backed by the issuer’s taxing power
A bond whose interest is always federally tax-exempt
A short-term note repaid by tax receipts
w: Correct: IDR bonds finance facilities leased to a company, and the lease payments back the debt.
Wrong: taxing power does not back IDRs; they are revenue-type bonds.
Wrong: IDRs benefit a private corporation and are generally taxable.
Wrong: IDRs are long-term bonds, not tax anticipation notes.

questions.q: Where can an investor find whether a municipal bond is subject to the alternative minimum tax (AMT)?
o: In the issuer’s trust indenture only
On the front cover of the official statement
On the customer’s new account form
In the issuer’s annual proxy statement
w: Wrong: AMT status is not disclosed only in the trust indenture.
Correct: the official statement’s front cover indicates AMT status, and the trade confirmation also discloses it.
Wrong: a new account form records customer data, not bond tax features.
Wrong: proxy statements relate to shareholder voting.

questions.q: Which investor is the LEAST suitable candidate for public purpose municipal bonds?
o: An executive in the highest tax bracket
A pension fund that is already tax-sheltered
A high-income investor seeking tax-free current income
w: Wrong: high-income buy-and-hold investors are the typical muni buyers.
Wrong: a high-bracket investor benefits most from tax-free interest.
Correct: tax-exempt interest adds nothing to an account that already shelters income, while accepting a lower yield.
Wrong: high-income investors seeking tax-free income are the natural audience.

questions.q: To be exempt from SEC registration under the Securities Act of 1933, commercial paper may have a maximum maturity of:
w: Wrong: 90 days is shorter than the limit; commercial paper may go further.
Wrong: 180 days is the typical maximum for banker’s acceptances, not commercial paper.
Wrong: one year is too long for the exemption.
Correct: commercial paper maturities may not exceed 270 days to qualify for the registration exemption.

questions.q: Which statement describes a negotiable certificate of deposit?
o: It has a minimum face value of $100,000 and can be sold to other investors
It can only be redeemed at the issuing bank
It is not considered a security
w: Correct: negotiable CDs are transferable securities with a $100,000 minimum face value.
Wrong: that describes a non-negotiable CD, which cannot be resold.
Wrong: negotiable CDs are securities and trade in the secondary market.
Wrong: CD interest is taxable.

questions.q: Mia buys a retail CD from her local bank that she cannot sell to anyone else. Which statement is true?
o: It is a security that trades in the money market
It is non-negotiable, is not considered a security and does not trade in the money market
It is a short-term municipal note
w: Wrong: because it cannot be traded, it is not a security and is not a money market instrument.
Correct: non-negotiable CDs can only be redeemed by the issuing bank and are not money market securities.
Wrong: banker’s acceptances are negotiable time drafts guaranteed by a bank.
Wrong: a CD is issued by a bank, not by a municipality.

questions.q: Banker’s acceptances were traditionally used to:
w: Wrong: BAs are debt instruments, not equity.
Wrong: municipal capital projects are financed with municipal bonds and notes.
Correct: importers used BAs, guaranteed by their banks, to pay exporters.
Wrong: mortgage pools are financed through MBS and CMOs.

questions.q: If the Federal Reserve wants to temporarily drain reserve balances from the banking system, it would most likely use:
w: Wrong: commercial paper is issued by corporations, not used by the Fed for monetary policy.
Wrong: repurchase agreements temporarily add reserve balances.
Wrong: BAs are trade finance instruments, not Fed policy tools.
Correct: reverse repos temporarily drain reserves, whereas repos temporarily add them.

questions.q: Which of the following can trade in the money market? I. A Treasury bond with eight months remaining to maturity II. An ADR III. A negotiable CD IV. Preferred stock
w: Correct: a Treasury bond with one year or less left and a negotiable CD qualify; equities do not.
Wrong: ADRs and preferred stock are equities, and no equities trade in the money market.
Wrong: this wrongly includes the ADR, which is an equity.
Wrong: neither ADRs nor preferred stock are money market instruments.
